title: System vaccinology analysis of predictors and mechanisms of antibody response durability to multiple vaccines in humans
one_line: A systems-vaccinology study identifying a day-7 platelet/megakaryocyte-derived blood transcriptional signature that predicts antibody response durability across multiple vaccines, and a megakaryocyte-dependent mechanism supporting bone marrow plasma cell survival.
key_claims: A day-7 post-vaccination blood transcriptional signature, dominated by platelet-derived transcripts and cell adhesion genes, predicts the longevity of antibody responses.
The signature generalised across six different vaccines in seven independent clinical trials, including COVID-19 mRNA, malaria, meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines.
Megakaryocytes support plasma cell survival in bone marrow via direct integrin-mediated cell contact plus APRIL and the MIF-CD74 axis.
TPO (thrombopoietin) activation of megakaryocytes enhanced antibody durability, suggesting a route to improve vaccine-induced immunity.
The AS03-adjuvanted H5N1 vaccine served as the primary discovery model system.
limitations: TPO enhancement of durability was not tested in human vaccination; timing, dosing and safety of platelet manipulation remain unaddressed.
The full nature of megakaryocyte-plasma cell interactions is not completely resolved.
Whether platelets themselves (as opposed to megakaryocytes) contribute to the immune response was not established.
Effects across different antibody response types/isotypes were not delineated.
Measurement of antibody durability is not standardised across the trials analysed.
open_questions: Does TPO administration around vaccination prolong antibody titres in a controlled human trial?
Can the day-7 platelet signature prospectively assign individuals to durable versus waning responses in a new cohort?
Which integrin and survival-factor pairs are strictly required for megakaryocyte-supported plasma cell survival in vivo?
